articles.title: Another rare, working Apple 1 signed by Steve Wozniak headed to auction
articles.summary: The Verge is about technology and how it makes us feel. Founded in 2011, we offer our audience everything from breaking news to reviews to award-winning features and investigations, on our site, in video, and in podcasts.
articles.body: Currently, there are estimated to only be six working models of the original Apple 1 left, and one of them is going up for auction in Germany on May 25th. Computerworld reports that it was originally purchased by one Fred Hatfield, who also received a letter signed by Steve Jobs offering an upgrade from the $666.66 Apple-1 to an Apple II 4K motherboard for another $400. According to Mike Willegal, who has tracked down many Apple 1 computers, this particular one had an interface for a selectric printer grafted onto it. Willegal also says that the reason for Jobs’ letter was that the original owner “complained to Apple about limited software availability.” The auction price for the computer is expected to land somewhere between $250,000 and $400,000 when it’s sold off — though strangely it apparently didn’t sell last year when it was put up for auction by the same company. We’ve seen a few Apple 1 computers sold at auction recently, with one sold in June of 2012 fetching $374,500 and another this past December for $640,000. Although this latest Apple 1 isn’t likely to hit those heights, it still has plenty going for it — it’s signed by Steve Wozniak, who built the motherboard by hand. Most importantly, it’s in complete working order, as the video posted by the auctioneer proves. The video shows the usual command line on the screen, as you’d expect, but also displays an ASCII-art image of Woz and Jobs printed across the screen.

articles.title: Android is becoming a worldwide earthquake detection network
articles.summary: Android phones will be able to detect earthquakes and, eventually, take part in an automated system that will provide early warning to millions of people worldwide. It will be built directly into the OS and work on the vast majority of phones.
articles.body: Google is creating a worldwide, Android phone-powered earthquake alert system. The first part of that system is rolling out today. If you opt in, the accelerometer in your Android phone will become one data point for an algorithm designed to detect earthquakes. Eventually, that system will automatically send warnings to people who could be impacted. It’s a feature made possible through Google’s strengths: the staggering numbers of Android phones around the world and clever use of algorithms on big data. As with its collaboration with Apple on exposure tracing and other Android features like car crash detection and emergency location services, it shows that there are untapped ways that smartphones could be used for something more important than doomscrolling. Google is rolling out the system in small stages. First, Google is partnering with the United States Geological Survey and the California Office of Emergency Services to send the agencies’ earthquake alerts to Android users in that state. Those alerts are generated by the already-existing ShakeAlert system, which uses data generated by traditional seismometers. “It’d be great if there were just seismometer-based systems everywhere that could detect earthquakes,” says Marc Stogaitis, principle Android software engineer at Google. But, he continues, “that’s not really practical and it’s unlikely to have global coverage because seismometers are extremely expensive. They have to be constantly maintained, you need a lot of them in an area to really have a good earthquake early warning system.” So the second and third stages of Google’s plan will be powered instead by Android phones. The company is proceeding fairly cautiously, though. In the second stage, Google will show localized results in Google searches for earthquakes based on the data it’s detecting from Android phones. The idea there is that when you feel an earthquake, you’ll go to Google to see if that’s what you felt or not. [Image: Before the stage where it sends alerts, Google will start by simply putting earthquake information in search results. Finally, once it has more confidence in the accuracy of the system, Google will begin actively sending out earthquake warnings to people who live in areas where there are not seismometer-based warning systems. Stogaitis says that the information collected as part of this program is “de-identified” from users and that Google only needs “coarse” location information for it to work. Both the earthquake alerts and the detection system are opt-in, as well. “What we really need for this is just these little mini seismometers that are out there,” Stogaitis says. “We don’t need to know anything about the person itself that’s sending it because that doesn’t matter.” An Android phone can become a “mini seismometer” because it has an accelerometer — the thing that detects if you’ve rotated it or not. Android’s system uses the data from that sensor to see if the phone is shaking. It only is on when an Android phone is plugged in and not in use, to preserve battery life. “We figured out [Android phones are] sensitive enough to detect earthquake waves. As an earthquake wave goes through, they’re able to detect them and usually see both key types of waves, the P wave and the S wave,” Stogaitis says. “Each phone is able to detect that something like an earthquake is happening, but then you need an aggregate of phones to know that for sure that it’s an earthquake happening.” [Image: The P wave (primary wave) is the first and fastest wave sent out from the epicenter of an earthquake. The S wave (secondary wave) is slower but can be much bigger. Google’s system is able to detect both. “Often people won’t even feel the P wave because it’s just smaller, while the S wave tends to cause a lot more damage,” Stogaitis says. “The P wave can be something that tells you to prepare for the S wave.” That data is processed in classic Google fashion: using algorithms on the aggregated data from thousands of phones to determine whether an earthquake is happening. Where traditional seismometers are expensive and precise, Android phones are cheap and numerous. Google can use Bayesian filters and other algorithms to turn those numbers into earthquake data that’s accurate enough for sending out warning alerts. Google says its system is capable of locating the epicenter and determining the strength of an earthquake. Even so, the basic physics of those waves means that there are limits to what’s possible, he explains: > The biggest key thing is that the phones that are nearest to the earthquake can help users away from the earthquake know about it. One of the limitations of the system is that we can’t warn all users before an earthquake reaches them. The users closest to the epicenter of the earthquake just aren’t likely to get a warning in time because we’re not predicting earthquakes ahead of time. That speed also means that Google’s Android-based warning system won’t have a human in the loop, since these warnings will range from “a couple of seconds” near the epicenter to 30 or 45 seconds on the outside. “We have many seismologists within the team who are literally just embedded with us,” Stogaitis says. That includes Richard Allen, “who spent most of his career on earthquake early warning [systems] and who did a lot of the design of ShakeAlert system, and who’s also kind of built a phone-based earthquake detection system in the past as well.” Allen’s MyShake app is an earlier example of a system like this — but the difference now is that Google can build that detection directly into Android and it can do it at Google’s scale. (Unlike Google’s system, MyShake works on iPhones.) Google’s intention is to have differing levels of alerts for different earthquakes. It has consulted with seismologists not only on the design of the core system but also on how the alerts should appear. The goal is to “convey information kind of as quickly as possible in a short amount of time so that users can understand that they need to react very quickly to an earthquake without reading a huge wall of text,” Stogaitis says. [Image: Google’s alerts will include very basic safety recommendations. Over the long term, Google hopes to create an API based on its earthquake detection system. It doesn’t plan on using this system on iPhones, but if the API comes out then Apple would be free to use it. More interesting, though, is what other systems would benefit from an earthquake detection API. > For example, somebody could build something that automatically stops an elevator at the next floor and opens the door so that people can get out before the wave comes. And you can turn off gas valves automatically, you can have something that stops medical procedures, or open the door to fire stations ahead of time. That’s a common problem in earthquakes where fires are a big deal and firefighters often just can’t get out. So, you can build something that does that. Airplanes can stop landing as they’re doing this, abort their landing. Trains can be slowed down. There’s an entire ecosystem that could be enabled by using this Android-based detection and having it sort of just publish server-side so that others can plug into it. The stakes for such a system would be incredibly high — and the responsibility for maintaining that system would be equally high. So that API is a long way off. Google’s plan is to minimize false positives and tune the system right now. Google also had to put in extensive effort to ensure its notifications wouldn’t overwhelm cellular networks. Sending out a ping to every Android phone all at once has the potential to clog up those airwaves. Google will be rolling this system out via Google Mobile Services, so it won’t require a full operating system update. This means both the detection system and the alerts should work on the vast majority of Android phones in use today. (It also means that these services won’t be coming to China anytime soon, as Android phones in that country do not use Google’s services.) Google is starting to provide earthquake alerts in California right away, using the existing seismometer network. Earthquake data will also begin showing up in Google searches soon as well. As for the warnings and alerts based on the data aggregated from Android phones, that will take a bit more time. Google says that if a region has an existing earthquake detection and warning system, its preference is to use that rather than the phone-based system. “Basically, there are hundreds of millions of people around the world that live near earthquake fault zones,” Stogaitis says, “and that’s something that we think we can help with.”

articles.title: Elon Musk tells advertisers: ‘Go fuck yourself’
articles.summary: Elon Musk said that the X ad boycott could kill his company, but he told advertisers to “stop” instead of trying to “blackmail me.”
articles.body: Elon Musk took the stage at the DealBook conference on Wednesday evening with nervous laughter and a cascade of jokes about himself and his companies. But the interview quickly turned to the more serious subject of Musk’s recent antisemitic posts on X (formerly Twitter) and whether his company can survive the advertiser boycott. On that matter, Musk seemed alternatingly apologetic and defiant — acknowledging his mistakes, then doing everything in his power to push advertisers away. “I hope they stop. Don’t advertise,” Musk told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin. “If somebody is going to try to blackmail me with advertising, blackmail me with money, go fuck yourself. Go fuck yourself. Is that clear? I hope it is.” He singled out Disney CEO Bob Iger, who discussed not wanting Disney to be affiliated with Musk while onstage earlier in the day. “Hey Bob, if you’re in the audience.” If advertisers don’t return, Musk said, “what this advertising boycott is going to do is it’s going to kill the company.” He seemed almost resigned to the possibility, speaking of it almost as though X were a martyr and advertisers the enemy. “That is what everybody on Earth will know,” he said. “We’ll be gone, and it’ll be gone because of an advertiser boycott.” [Media: Musk’s message to advertisers came after what had briefly appeared to be an attempt to salvage the damage he caused after he called an antisemitic post the “actual truth” two weeks ago. More than 100 brands have since halted their ads, and the company is at risk of losing $75 million by the end of the year, according to The New York Times. “I should in retrospect should not have replied to that one person,” Musk said. He blamed media outlets for not covering his clarifications before apologizing. “Essentially I handed a loaded gun to those who hate me, and arguably to those are antisemitic, and for that I’m quite sorry. That was not my intention.” But even in his attempts to explain himself — that out of tens of thousands of posts on X, he’s bound to say “foolish” things — Musk insisted he wasn’t on an “apology tour.” He said his recent visit to Israel wasn’t in response to the criticism of his posts and that he didn’t mind being an object of contempt. He then went on a rambling explanation of what he says he really meant: his belief that Jewish people are funding causes meant to “annihilate” them. His attempted clarification only seemed to further the antisemitic conspiracy theory he promoted in the first place, broadly blaming “people in the Jewish community” for their support of unnamed activist groups. X CEO Linda Yaccarino — the former advertising chief at NBCUniversal who Musk brought on board to shore up the platform’s appeal to advertisers — took to X shortly after her CTO’s rant to say this: “Here’s my perspective when it comes to advertising: X is standing at a unique and amazing intersection of Free Speech and Main Street — and the X community is powerful and is here to welcome you. To our partners who believe in our meaningful work — Thank You.” The full interview was meandering and at times devolved into stream of consciousness responses; Musk spoke for triple the time most other interviewees did. But the questions around Musk’s own actions, and the resulting advertiser exodus — the things that could materially impact X — seemed to garner the most nonchalant answers. He doesn’t seem to care. Update November 30th, 4:35AM ET: Added statement from X CEO Linda Yaccarino.

articles.title: This watch has Pong and Missile Command instead of apps
articles.summary: The Atari 2600 My Play Watch is a fitness tracker with four playable retro games: Pong, Missile Command, Super Breakout, and Centipede.
articles.body: Atari is now selling a smartwatch that prioritizes fun over functionality. The watch’s user interface can be customized with Atari 2600-themed artwork and sound effects. But pushing it squarely into impulse purchase territory is the watch’s ability to play Centipede, Pong, Super Breakout, and Missile Command using the touchscreen or the watch’s crown dial functioning as a paddle controller. Instead of trying to compete with the Apple Watch’s capabilities, the Atari 2600 My Play Watch targets longtime gamers nostalgic enough for the consoles of their youth to spend $79.99 on an elaborately themed fitness tracker. The watch is available for preorder now through Atari’s online store and is expected to ship by June 10th, 2025. [Image: If the Atari 2600 My Play Watch feels familiar, it’s because it’s actually based on the Space Invaders My Play Watch that launched last September through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign. Its limited smartwatch capabilities are nearly identical to that previous version, including swappable watch faces and fitness tracking capabilities like step tracking, calories burned, and a heart rate monitor. There’s still no Bluetooth or Wi-fi connectivity. So, while the Atari 2600 My Play Watch won’t pester you with notifications from your smartphone, you won’t be able to expand its capabilities by downloading apps or new games. [Image: Is squinting at your wrist the ideal way to play Super Breakout? There are a few upgrades on the Atari 2600 My Play Watch. Its 2.02-inch touchscreen is slightly larger than the 1.86-inch screen on the Space Invaders watch, it has a beefier and more industrial-looking metal case, and there’s now a button located beneath its crown dial. It also comes with three swappable bands featuring retro graphic designs, although Atari says they will only be available for a limited time.

articles.title: DJI ban: how the world’s biggest dronemaker is getting shoved out of the US
articles.summary: DJI will be banned from the US on December 23rd by law, stopping all imports of new tech, unless US government agencies or Trump step in at the last minute.
articles.body: December 23rd, 2025. That’s the day DJI was automatically to be banned from the United States — until the FCC did it a day ahead of schedule. You’ll still be able to fly your existing DJI drones and film with existing Osmo cameras. But DJI will be barred from importing any new products into the US, and the FCC can retroactively ban imports of old DJI products too, after a waiting period. Not just drones, by the way — anything with a wireless radio. Why a ban? Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle claim to be worried the Chinese company is spying on us, even though the US government has never publicly provided evidence of that. Some worry China could compel the company to turn over drone data. (DJI has denied it shares any data with China, claims it stores all such data in the US and announced it would delete all US flight logs in September 2024.) Some also suggest DJI wouldn’t need to be compelled because DJI is allegedly “owned by the Chinese Communist Party,” though a US judge decided there wasn’t enough evidence to back that up in September 2025. Either way, lawmakers and Trump would clearly prefer that American drones “dominate” the skies rather than Chinese ones, and it’s true that DJI’s drones dominate today. No other company has been able to produce similarly a volume of high-quality, low-cost drones, to the point that some Republican lawmakers finally began to push back against a ban just weeks before the December 2025 deadline. They argued that DJI drones are important for farmers, energy companies, and rescue workers since no viable alternatives exist. Most of of DJI’s old competitors, like Skydio, have pivoted to enterprise and military — the new Insta360/Antigravity A1 is an unusual exception. Even without a ban, DJI was already on the rails. US customs has been blocking many of its drone imports for over a year, seemingly claiming that DJI was using forced labor to produce its drones. (DJI denies this.) Between import scrutiny, increased tariffs and the broader political situation, most of its products had disappeared from store shelves; it didn’t even bother to launch its flagship Mavic 4 Pro, Mini 5 Pro, and Neo 2 in the US. Instead, it appears DJI has been looking to sneak its products into the US under other brand names, like Xtra for cameras, or Skyrover for consumer drones, though the FCC will likely be able to crack down on those as well. To avoid the ban, “an appropriate national security agency” would have needed to audit DJI and decide it’s not a threat, but DJI said no agency had ever taken up the task. It’s always possible Trump will change the government’s mind. Remember the TikTok ban? Trump pressed pause on that one, despite it being signed into law, and those lawmakers seem to have no idea what might happen next. But he didn’t do so before the FCC stepped in. We’ll let you know what happens next in this StoryStream.

articles.title: This Tetris-playing watch struggles with the one thing it should be great at
articles.summary: The Tetris: My Play Watch does a great job at celebrating the game with extensive theming, but actually playing Tetris is disappointingly frustrating.
articles.body: The Tetris: My Play Watch may look like an Apple Watch, but it eschews most of the functionality you’ll typically find on a smartwatch to focus on two things: playing Tetris and celebrating the game through a UI that’s thoroughly Tetris-themed. It’s very good at making you want to play Alexey Pajitnov’s iconic tetromino-stacking puzzler, just not on the watch because of frustrating touchscreen controls that require more focus than the game itself. The included straps are colorfully Tetris-themed (you can swap them with standard watch straps if you want to tone it down), as is the collection of nine different faces. There are both digital and analog options with different themes and colors that display a mix of various metrics, including battery life and fitness stats. They all manage to work tetromino pieces and the Tetris logo into their designs, but there’s no customizability. [Image: The Tetris theming is carried forward to swappable bands, but you can attach a standard strap for a subtler look. The watch’s interface is navigated using its touchscreen and a side crown dial that’s pressed or rotated to make selections or to scroll lists. There aren’t any other buttons, but you wouldn’t need them since the watch’s functionality is so limited. From the main menu, you can play Tetris or use other features that include a stopwatch, timer, calendar, calculator, fitness tracker, and alarm. They’re all very basic. You can set multiple alarms, for example, but you can’t customize when they repeat or choose anything other than the main Tetris theme with gentle vibrations to alert you. Even the Game Boy version of Tetris that launched 36 years ago had alternate themes to choose from. [Image: There are nine different Tetris-themed watch faces to choose from, but aside from various metrics that update, the faces are all static. There’s a heart rate sensor that matched readings from my Apple Watch Series 9, but the other fitness tracking metrics are limited. There’s step counting with an adjustable daily goal and stride length options to improve accuracy, and an estimation of the calories you’ve burned that resets every night. There’s no history, no proactive health warnings, and no notifications at all because the watch lacks Bluetooth and Wi-Fi and doesn’t connect to your smartphone. [Image: If you want the look of an Apple Watch without any of the distractions or advanced health tracking, the Tetris watch is a close facsimile. It’s an upgrade over a traditional digital watch and could be an option for someone who wants the look of a smartwatch without notifications. But anyone considering spending $79.99 on it is buying it to play Tetris. Unfortunately, it’s not a great implementation. Previous versions of the My Play Watch used the crown dial to play retro games like Space Invaders and Breakout, but the Tetris version is played only via the touchscreen. When the watch was announced in September, I was worried that touch controls “could prove challenging on a small screen for those chasing high scores,” but it turns out the controls make even just quick play sessions frustrating. [Image: The watch offers two Tetris gameplay modes, Marathon and Puzzle, and features like previews of upcoming pieces and silhouettes of where your piece will land. You move pieces by dragging your finger across the screen from side to side, rotate them by tapping, increase their fall rate by tapping and holding, or immediately drop them onto the stack below with a downward swipe. The gestures are easy enough to learn, but I found the watch’s touchscreen would either regularly not detect them or misinterpret what I was doing. Short finger slides meant to reposition a piece by a few cells were frequently detected as a tap, resulting in an unwanted rotation. On more than one occasion, when I quickly tapped in a panic to rotate it back, the watch would interpret the gesture as a downward swipe and drop the piece where I didn’t want it. There are options in the game’s settings that try to make the touch controls easier to use, including auto-rotate, which predicts the best orientation for a piece based on what’s below it. But accidental spins still happen and often mess up your game. Playing Tetris on the watch isn’t impossible, but because of the frustrating touch controls, I found myself focusing more on carefully executing taps and swipe gestures than any kind of stacking strategy. It increased the challenge, but not in the way any Tetris fan would want. Equally disappointing is that the control issues I experienced can’t be remedied through software updates, since the watch isn’t capable of getting any. Even something simple, like limiting rotations to taps on the edges of the screen, would help, but it’s a change that can only be implemented in future versions of the watch. [Image: Even the charging indicator, which you’ll probably be seeing a lot, is Tetris-themed with a battery that slowly fills with neatly stacked tetrominoes. Battery life isn’t great, either. I’m already used to charging my Apple Watch every night, but you need to limit your playtime to get a full day’s use from the Tetris watch. During my first day of testing, I maxed out the brightness and volume, and with less than 15 minutes of playing Tetris, the watch’s battery drained in 6.5 hours. Reducing the brightness to its lowest setting and halving the volume doubled its battery life to about 12 hours. The battery lost about 6 percent of its charge while playing Tetris for five minutes. I like the idea of a wearable version of Tetris that I can quickly play without distracting notifications. It’s a game that relaxes my brain and is a nice stress reliever, but this version had the opposite effect. You may still be tempted to strap one on if you want the world to know how much you love the game. If you want fun, look elsewhere.

articles.title: Billionaires are making empty threats to leave California if they’re asked to hoard slightly less money.
articles.summary:
There’s a proposal making the rounds in California to levy a 5 percent wealth tax on anyone worth more than $1 billion. The proposal isn’t guaranteed to make it to the ballot next year. Just like when Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor of New York, lots of the ultra-wealthy are having a hissy fit. But it seems highly unlikely that Larry Page is going to take his $258 billion (more than the GDP of most countries) and leave his longtime home for the corn fields of Nebraska. The New York Times points out that:
> The potential wealth tax is under debate as the income divide in the United States becomes increasingly stark. Recent data from the Congressional Budget Office showed that income inequality increased over a 33-year period ending in 2022, with the share of wealth held by families in the top 10 percent at around 69 percent, while the share held by families in the bottom 50 percent at just 3 percent.

articles.title: Intel Panther Lake laptop CPU review: call it a comeback
articles.summary: Intel’s Core Ultra X9 388H Panther Lake laptop CPU, the first on the new 18A process, has been hyped up for months. We’ve tested it in a new Asus Zenbook Duo.
articles.body: Intel’s been talking the talk for months about its new generation of laptop chips, the first made on its long-anticipated 18A process. 18A is meant to steer Intel back toward bluer waters by making its chips better, and, if possible, attracting chip designers like Qualcomm and Nvidia to use Intel’s foundries, not just its rival TSMC’s. Last year’s Arrow Lake chips received a mixed reception, particularly desktop versions. The mobile-only Lunar Lake chips, on the other hand, were great, showing that the x86 architecture still has plenty of fight in it against a slowly rising tide of Arm-based Windows laptops. But Lunar Lake was a one-off that Intel designed more than manufactured, relying on TSMC silicon to do the heaviest lifting. Panther Lake puts homegrown Intel inside once again. I’ve been testing the flagship Intel Core Ultra X9 388H Panther Lake chip in the 2026 Asus Zenbook Duo dual-screen laptop, and it’s been a treat. It’s fast enough for intensive work and multitasking, powerful enough for 1080p gaming at high settings, and lasts well over a full workday using productivity apps on battery power. With Panther Lake, Intel is walking the walk. [Image: We tested Panther Lake in the $2,300 Asus Zenbook Duo laptop. Panther Lake CPUs come in 8- and 16-core versions, made up of Cougar Cove performance cores (P-cores) and Darkmont efficiency cores (E-cores). The Core Ultra X9 388H in the Zenbook Duo is the top-tier 16-core model with an Intel Arc B390 GPU (consisting of 12 Xe graphics cores), a base power of 25W and a maximum turbo power up to 80W. Intel hyped it as more efficient than Lunar Lake while simultaneously more powerful than the Arrow Lake chips that are typically found in higher-power workstation and desktop replacement laptops. Against its closest competition, Panther Lake isn’t an outright winner. Most benchmark scores in our table below are dominated by Apple’s M5 and AMD’s top-tier Strix Halo. But the Intel 388H Panther Lake chip handily beats AMD’s highest-end Strix Point chip in all but one of the tests we ran. That’s a solid leapfrogging by Intel, considering Strix Point handily beat Lunar Lake just a year ago. Now, Panther Lake also trounces our examples of both Lunar Lake and Arrow Lake-H. While Apple is still the speed champ in most of these categories, I was pleasantly surprised to see Panther Lake slightly edge out the MacBook Pro in our 4K video export in Adobe Premiere Pro. That’s those 12 graphics cores at work. In real-world use, Panther Lake’s speed is palpable. When I fired up my Adobe Lightroom Classic catalog and started editing some of my 50-megapixel RAW files, it felt as quick — or nearly as quick — as a MacBook Pro. I could make heavy-handed changes in the Develop module, and bounce around between images, without everything bogging down as it often does on other Windows laptops. Even subject detection and healing brush removal were snappy. And I did my photo editing on battery power. Unlike most Windows laptops I’ve used up till now, the Zenbook Duo is just about as fast on battery power as it is connected to the wall. This is often something that Windows laptop makers restrict in their hardware designs, but I’m relieved it’s not the case with Panther Lake on the Zenbook Duo. It’s a big win for editing and content creation on Windows, as it lets the platform match one of the major strengths of modern MacBooks. I just hope all Windows laptop manufacturers follow suit. [Image: [Image: Speaking of battery power, Panther Lake in the Zenbook Duo is a champ. Especially when you consider it’s powering two bright, high-resolution OLED displays. You can read deeper details on my real-world experience with the Zenbook Duo’s battery life in my full review of the laptop, but here are a couple quick hits: It lasted over 14 hours in our rundown test, and I could easily last a nine-hour workday of dual-screen multitasking with enough juice left over for some lighter casual use in the evening. As for gaming, Intel claims that Panther Lake’s 12 Xe graphics cores are on par with Nvidia’s discrete RTX 4050 laptop GPU, much like how Strix Halo goes toe-to-toe with the RTX 4060. Digital Foundry’s early testing at CES found Panther Lake to be nipping at the heels of a desktop RTX 3050 card at 1080p resolution. [Image: The Intel Graphics Software app is where you can choose your XeSS multi-frame generation override, as well as download graphics driver updates. I only did a handful of scripted gaming benchmarks, because I wanted to spend more time actually playing. But one benchmark that stood out to me was Cyberpunk 2077, which averaged 40fps at 1920 x 1200 resolution on Ultra settings. That’s without ray tracing, but also without any XeSS (Intel’s version of super resolution upscaling). Panther Lake is no slouch, even if AMD’s beefy Strix Halo chip still has the edge on graphics. Once I dove into playing titles like Cyberpunk, Helldivers 2, Battlefield 6, and a few others, I discovered that Panther Lake can typically hit 60fps or slightly below at 1920 x 1200 resolution on High settings with XeSS Balanced enabled. You can push the graphics quality further by turning on ray tracing or flipping XeSS from Balanced to Quality, but I’d only do that if you’re comfortable playing closer to 30fps. I prefer 60fps as my baseline. Setting game graphics to hit a baseline of 40 to 60fps means you can flip on the new XeSS multi-frame generation, which can make games look buttery smooth at well above 120fps. You can control multi-frame generation in Intel’s app, and pick between 2x, 3x, and 4x frame generation. It felt smooth enough to use in Battlefield 6 and got close to the Zenbook Duo’s native 144Hz refresh (though I turn it off in multiplayer to ensure there’s no chance of increased input latency). Nvidia may be marching on toward 6x Multi Frame Generation with DLSS 4.5, but Intel’s doing a fine job on its slower cadence — and it’s still ahead of AMD’s Redstone, which doesn’t support multi-frame gen. [Image: Cyberpunk 2077 running on its High preset in 1920 x 1200 resolution, with XeSS set to Quality and 3x frame generation. “Fake frames” are fine in my book for single-player games. [Image: Battlefield 6 running at 1920 x 1200 resolution, Medium preset with Balanced XeSS, and resolution scaling set to 75 percent. This ensured mostly 60+ fps without frame generation. As excited as I am for Panther Lake to finally arrive, and to stick its landing this well, I’m now looking forward to further testing of slightly lower-end versions — ones found in more moderately priced laptops than this $2,300 dual-screen with a massive battery. (A handheld, perhaps?) And I’m equally excited to see how new contenders from AMD and Qualcomm stack up, including those cheaper gaming-focused Strix Halo variants. It’s an exciting time for new laptop releases (rising prices aside, of course). There’s plenty of upcoming competition, but Panther Lake is first out of the gate and looking like the Windows laptop chip to beat. Welcome back to the show, Intel.

articles.title: How to Build a ‘Friday the 13th’ Prequel: Blood Bags, Old-School Paranoia, and Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees
articles.summary: Star Cardellini and showrunner Brad Caleb Kane scare up a hell of a good "Friday the 13th" prequel. They tell IndieWire how '70s paranoia, their own horror p...
articles.body:
It's interesting, to this day, how many people still don't realize Jason Voorhees only appears for a brief second in the original "Friday the 13th" film. Spoiler for a 46-year-old film (and the opening scene of "Scream" and the entire premise of the new "Friday the 13th" prequel series): Jason's mother, Pamela Voorhees, is the killer in the first film.

In the 1980 film directed by Sean S. Cunningham, we know Pamela Voorhees blames pretty much everyone at Camp Crystal Lake for the drowning death of her son, Jason Voorhees (we assume you are familiar with his work), and goes on a murderous rampage (which includes a young Kevin Bacon). The new series explores, well, how did it get to this point?

"Crystal Lake" has been in some sort of development, off and on, for around 23 years . The rights to "Friday the 13th" are mired in an extremely complicated legal situation, with different entities owning different aspects of what Jason Voorhees would become. (For example, Jason doesn't have his iconic hockey mask until the third installment, and there are legal claims on that creation versus what we see in the first film.)

But "Crystal Lake," with its '70s backdrop, is a long way off from anyone running around with a hockey mask. But! Here we are, finally , with Brad Caleb Kane getting this show made. And, now, coming off her Emmy win for "DTF St. Louis," Linda Cardellini in the lead role of Pamela Voorhees.

Ahead, Kane and Cardellini share what each wanted from the Pamela Voorhees we see in this series, and why the show added a conspiratorial subplot that didn't exist in the films. (Oh, and a lot of praise for Don Knotts, who we do see in the series, kind of surprisingly.)

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When Linda was cast, you didn't realize you were getting Emmy winner Linda Cardellini.

Brad Caleb Kane: No! But she should have already had an Emmy by the time I cast her for "Crystal Lake." But I did know that all of her performances are indelible and amazing. She has an effortless likability. One of the things I was thinking when I first reached out to Linda to talk to her about possibly taking on the part was her performance in "Dead to Me," holding everything that she knows inside and not being able to reveal to a person what she's done. That element of holding all of that information inside and making us see, without commenting on it, how much it's paining her and how conflicted she is. That was a real element we needed for our Pamela Voorhees. Somebody who is keeping secrets, but you can see it is eating away inside of her. And transforms into a person that just lets her freak flag fly, joyfully. So I wanted that quality and she does it effortlessly in that show, so that's why I reached out.

This series was first discussed as far back as 2003.

Sean S. Cunningham mentioned he had an idea in development. Over the years, so many people have tried. How did you do it?

Kane: Right place, right time. Right take for the right people.

And I realize this has had a very complicated legal journey.

Kane: Yeah, all that stuff is kind of above my paygrade — all the legal wrangling that went on to sort of pull all the rights together. I think that happened with A24 and Jason Inc. I think there's another rights holder? And some people have the rights to the mask but not the name. All that stuff was done and dealt with before I came on board and pitched my take. It really was just a function of me seeing they were going to make this thing.

The great Bryan Fuller, who I am a massive fan of, had, I guess, creative differences with some of the people. And he ended up going in a different direction. But they were looking to make it with somebody because they did want to do a Pamela Voorhees prequel and, when I saw that was happening, I reached out because "Friday the 13th Part III," it was the first "Friday the 13th" I saw in theaters.

That was 1982, right? That was my first one, but I didn't really get into these until the pandemic. I found them comforting.

Kane: Right. And I remember a full crowd and the manipulation of that crowd and them yelling at the screen. There was a fine layer of marijuana smoke over everybody's head with the blue beam of the projector cutting through it. It's all very proustian for me.

Kane: Yeah, totally! Shelly Finkelstein with his props! That guy is a lawyer now. I think he's a lawyer for some of the people who were in the various movies. Because the "Friday the 13th" universe is a small family, people reach out from other movies and stuff. And I think he's actually a lawyer for some of those people. The actors from various movies. He's made "Friday the 13th" representation a career.

Linda, what's your prior relationship with "Friday the 13th"?

Linda Cardellini: I mean, I saw the movies when I was a kid. I loved scary movies when I was a kid. I think it made me seem cool, I felt like, to my older brother. I saw other ones in the theaters, but I do remember seeing "Freddy vs. Jason" in the theaters. It was in LA at Universal City Walk and it was packed . And people were screaming at the screen! I was waiting for that movie to come out. They were two icons, two worlds colliding. So I love a Halloween horror night. I mean, less so now, I'm a little bit older, but I really love the thrill and the fun of it.

And I'm a big Halloween lover. Halloween the holiday. So, all that stuff I think is really fun. I mean, you can't really even think about the date Friday the 13th without seeing the mask in your mind, or wondering about how auspicious that date is. So I think it just worked its way in for a child of the '80s — it worked your way into your psyche. The same way you feel scared when you go into a pool and there might be a shark there. [ Laughs ] Because we saw "Jaws"!

Kane: To your point about finding them comforting during the pandemic, a lot of that has to do with the nostalgia factor of it and that yearning of a simpler time…

Yes, a simpler time when Jason Vorhees would run around and stab people.

Kane: You step onto the camp grounds and this guy is going to get you. And probably in a very inventive and creative way.

Kane: Totally over the top. And there's something very comforting about going back to those things of our youth that were simpler than things are now — in our personal lives or the world at large. So, yeah, that is why they are comforting in a lot of ways.

Cardellini: And it not being hyper-realistic, too, that is fun about it. That part of it makes it entertainment to digest.

Are you surprised by how many people don't realize that Jason basically isn't even in the first movie?

Kane: That exact thing is what got Drew Berrymore killed at the beginning of Scream. She got that answer wrong! I don't know, do people not know now that Mrs. Voorhees was the killer in the first movie?

I think the average citizen at large does not know that.

Cardellini: And you think the hockey mask was there all along, too.

Right. Which doesn't show up until the end of the third one.

Kane: Well, we should educate them. [ Laughs ] I like to think of myself as an educator.

Linda has a scene where she wraps a guy's head in a clear plastic bag, who has a head wound, then the bag completely fills with blood and explodes onto your face.

Cardellini: When I read that, I was very excited. Because that's an inventive way to see this happen. Not realizing, oh, wait a minute, I'll be covered in that from head to toe.

Kane: Oh, you didn't realize the reality of it on the ground?

Cardellini: No, but I thought it was so fun and inventive and strange and I love that about parts of the show. We took a week to shoot that sequence. Is it like a 15-minute sequence?

Cardellini: It's a 20-minute sequence and there's not very much talking.

Cardellini: And she's just being put through it physically. To me, I loved that about it. That it wasn't dialogue-heavy and that it was really about … ah … that it was cinematic to me. It read cinematic to me and I thought that would be a lot of fun and I hadn't done anything like that before. After, I think that is such a great tableau for her, looking in the mirror, "What did you do?" And being at that point in her life, it sets you on the road for what you're about to see. And how does she become that person.

Kane: And all of that stuff is just a function of her trying to survive. None of that is gratuitous, "Oh, let's show you a whole bunch of blood." She was trying to survive. She does what she does…

Cardellini: She's trying to clean it up!

Kane: She's trying to clean it up and not turn it into this mess and it turns into this thing. It's the escalating situations of growing absurdity.

And we feel a lot of empathy for Jason in the flashbacks and how he's treated, I never thought I'd say that sentence.

Kane: I'm one of those people who believes, concretely, that monsters are not born. They are made. There might be some genetic predisposition or some chemical thing that may be going on, then turned on. I wanted to show that monsters like Jason and Pamela were not monsters to begin with. They were formed by certain circumstances and situations and manipulations.

We come to TV for character. We want to spend time with characters. We want to get to know them and we want to empathize with them. And, obviously, Jason and Pamala Voorhees are our main characters in this franchise. So how do you empathize with them? Well, you have to show them as human beings.

There's a conspiratorial aspect and mystery to this show that isn't really present in the films…

Kane: We set the show in the '70s, because the first movie was 1980…

Right, Pamela Voorhees is watching Don Knotts on TV.

Kane: Don Knotts! Yes! The Don Knotts variety show. I'm a big "The Ghost and Mr. Chicken" fan. Legitimately, not ironically.

Kane: I like "The Incredible Mr. Limpet," but seeing Don Knotts' voice come out of that fish is not as exciting.

I was big into "The Apple Dumpling Gang."

Kane: I grew up on that. Well, now we're just talking Don Knotts…

Kane: But, if you're going to set something in the '70s, specifically, what was so prominent that decade — the movies that were prominent and the feeling that was in the air. For America, the feeling in the '70s that was really prominent was mistrust in institutions. You see that in the movies that are really popular at the time, specifically the Alan Pakula paranoid thrillers trilogy. "Klute," "The Parallax View," "All the President's Men." Even movies like "Three Days of the Condor." So it felt like, if we are going to do a show that takes place in the '70s, let's bring that aspect to it. Let's have Pamela and Jason be on the run from something and have it parallel the things that were going on in America at the time.

There's been a lot of speculation I've seen online, "Oh, is he making Jason a supersoldier?" "Is this a 'Stranger Things'?" "Is this 'Jason XI'?" It's none of that. It's nothing that's out of the realm of reality. It's all stuff that's based in science and things that were going on at the time. He's not a genetically engineered anything. That conspiracy that we learn about later in the season comes out of a very specific human instinct that Pamela has, that's been turned on its head and turned into manipulation and gaslighting and all the things that women and America had to go through at this time in American history.

I'm going to embarrass Linda now, but we had what we had on the page, and I say this legitimately, the show doesn't work unless you have an actor who approaches this character seriously and with respect. And the spirit of creating a real situation under these imaginary circumstances. And she came to work and she put in the thought behind it…

And in her last show, she singlehandedly brought back the phrase, "No way, Jose."

All eight episodes of "Crystal Lake" start streaming on Peacock on Thursday, October 15.

articles.title: Google is making inline links more prominent in AI responses
articles.summary: Google is updating its AI search results to make inline links appear “higher up in responses more frequently” and announcing several other updates to highlight links and publishers.
articles.body: Google is updating its AI search results to make inline links appear “higher up in responses more frequently,” according to a blog post. The company’s search results from AI Overviews and AI Mode give you answers in a customized view instead of the traditional list of links, but there are concerns that the format reduces traffic to publishers. Google says it’s been making “continued and substantial increases to the presence of inline links in our AI experiences,” and this new change will help ensure “ensure key sources are easily clickable right when you need them.” The company is announcing several other changes to highlight links and publishers within its AI results. For sites that are among a few for a specific task or certain information — an example image from Google highlights a query about an airline refund — Google is testing showing the relevant links at the top of a response with context. For “timely” articles, the company is now rolling out the link carousels announced in May to more locations and languages. Google is making links at the end of a query “more engaging and prominent, with image thumbnails and a more clickable design.” And it’s now testing clickable links in AI mode to search profiles for publishers and creators. [Image: An image from Google showing relevant links to a query about getting a refund. Google also says that more than 400 publishers are participating in its “News AI” pilot program, which it announced in December. The licensing program pays publishers for “the delivery and use of enhanced content to develop new AI features,” including “in-depth article overviews on Google News publisher pages,” and Axios, CNN, and the Financial Times are among the partners that are newly onboard, according to Google.

articles.title: Volvo will use Nvidia’s tech for hands-free, point-to-point driving
articles.summary: Volvo said it will introduce a hands-free, point-to-point partially automated driving system using Nvidia’s AI technology stack.
articles.body: Volvo plans to launch hands-free, point-to-point driving by 2030, powered by Nvidia’s latest AI technology. The Chinese-owned, Swedish-designed automaker said Thursday it would use Nvidia’s autonomous driving stack to power a new partially automated driving system similar to Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised). Volvo says the new point-to-point system will be Level 2++, meaning it can handle complex urban environments, including traffic lights, stop signs, and unprotected left turns without explicit driver control. In addition to Tesla’s FSD, it will also resemble the Nvidia-powered system that Mercedes-Benz recently rolled out for the all-new CLA sedan, said Ali Kani, VP and general manager of the automotive team at Nvidia, in an interview with The Verge. Volvo will use Nvidia’s Hyperion platform, which includes the chipmaker’s high-powered silicon, as well as additional sensors mounted around the vehicle so the car can see and perceive its surroundings. The automaker will also utilize Nvidia’s Alpamayo software, which uses “reasoning” models to make sense of complex road conditions and plan where to steer, brake, or accelerate. The setup will not include lidar, though it could include the laser sensor if Volvo decides to add it in the future. By expanding its preexisting partnership with Volvo, the automaker is trying to correct some of its failed automated driving projects of the past. The automaker had to effectively sideline its Ride Pilot Level 3 unsupervised autonomous driving system in the US after failing to obtain regulatory approval. Volvo also planned to add lidar sensors to some of its models, but that plan fell away after its supplier Luminar went bankrupt. Volvo is also bringing its own reputation for safety to the table. The automaker wants to combine its safety expertise with Nvidia’s technology to improve the overall system, including contributing its proprietary driver-understanding systems, which analyze driver behavior in considerably greater detail than a basic driver monitoring system, said Alwin Bakkenes, head of global software engineering at Volvo Cars. “Our brand Volvo is synonymous with safety, and safety is synonymous with trust,” Bakkenes said in an interview. “People get into our cars not expecting anything bad to happen, but they feel intrinsically that if they’re ever in a situation … we will do our utmost to keep people safe, to protect them from harm.” Another important component is Volvo’s connected safety technology that allows its vehicles to exchange information about hazards and conditions ahead, including roadworks. Sharing this information can effectively extend the system’s awareness beyond what an individual vehicle’s sensors can detect, potentially improving the operating capabilities of the self-driving functionality. Volvo plans to make the new point-to-point driving system available across its vehicle lineup, from entry-level to high-end versions — though the company didn’t reveal which models will come first. The timeline was also a little vague, with Bakkenes only confirming that it will launch “before the end of the decade.” Kani also pointed to the commercial implications, noting that point-to-point driving may prove to be more valuable than a system limited to highway assistance. Nvidia sees the partnership as an opportunity not only to advance the technology but also to help Volvo develop its business model around ongoing software-based offerings, he said.

articles.title: Sony made a $5,900 gold-plated Walkman MP3 player
articles.summary: Sony’s $6,000 media player slathered is gold is the perfect gift for the gaudy millionaire audiophile in your life.
articles.body: Sony has announced a trio of new Walkman portable media players that start at an already absurd $1,899.99 for the NW-ZX900 and climb all the way up to $5,899 for the gold-plated NW-WM1ZM3. Sandwiched in between is the $2,999.99 Walkman NW-WM1AM3, which is nearly identical to the WM1ZM3, just minus the gaudy gold shell. All three devices are aimed squarely at the audiophile market, if the price tag didn’t make that clear. All three feature Sony’s DSD (Direct Stream Digital) Remastering Engine, which upsamples standard PCM audio to an 11.2MHz DSD stream, which it claims delivers a more analog-like sound. They also all feature gold-plating on the rear chassis that’s meant to reduce interference and lower noise. The higher-end Walkman NW-WM1ZM3 and NW-WM1AM3 add hand-soldered oxygen-free copper (OFC) wiring and upgraded power circuitry to lower noise even further. A milled OFC block isolates the digital circuits from the analog ones to limit potential interference. What sets the WM1ZM3 apart is that the entire chassis is made of OFC and then gold-plated. This is not the first time Sony has gone all out on a gold media player. In fact, you can pick up the previous model — the NW-WM1ZM2 — on sale now for just $2,599.99. A veritable steal. Though, an old iPod bought off eBay is still probably the better bargain.

articles.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt, Amazon devices chief Panos Panay described a future where ambient AI devices work in the background, anticipating users' needs instead of waiting for commands.
articles.body:
Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI.

Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.

“A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.”

By “ambient devices,” he means those that work quietly in the background, using sensors and AI to help you figure out what needs to be done, instead of the other way around, where you’re telling the device what you need to do.

“As it works in the background, you’re able to stay more present. You’re able to get more done. You’re about to spend more time with people … you’re not afraid if you miss something. It’s incredibly powerful,” Panay said.

Amazon’s biggest entry into this space is the set of new Bee devices it introduced on Thursday, which include a band you can wear on your wrist or detach to wear as a pendant, as well as a new credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of your smartphone.

These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to. To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done. Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls. That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.

Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work.

“You have to give customers that control,” he said. “Every product is different, but for Bee specifically, as an example in the ambient space like that, you have to design with privacy in mind. And that’s what we do. That’s critical.”

The executive, who came to Amazon after 19 years at Microsoft where he oversaw the development of Surface devices, has spent a lot of his life thinking about how personal computing will evolve. With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.

“Do I think we have a future where there’s a bit of a balance — a whole generation that doesn’t say ‘give me the app’ for that, but says it should just understand what I need? Yeah, I do. I think that transformation is coming. I think that is the next generation,” he said.

That doesn’t necessarily mean the smartphone itself won’t continue to be an important personal computing device (as much as Amazon would like it to be an Alexa tablet or Echo smart speaker), Panay pointed out. Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you.

“I’m not a proponent that says one form factor is going to replace another. I don’t think that’s the case,” he clarified. “I think there’s an intelligence layer that connects it all … and it has to be useful.”

articles.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay on the importance of failure and bouncing back from it  | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Panay said that it's possible to recover and learn from all sorts of failures, even catastrophic ones, when building products.
articles.body:
Amazon executive Panos Panay has a message for startup founders: Failure is an inevitable, required part of building a successful product.

Panay, Amazon SVP of Devices, Alexa, and Leo, shared that advice onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, drawing on his own experience at Microsoft, where he spent more than 19 years and weathered one particularly expensive failure.

“You have to be willing to fail, and actually, not just willing, you actually have to go fail,” Panay said. “If you haven’t failed, you probably haven’t pushed the boundary. It’s literally about harvesting the lessons learned when you fail. You have to be willing to face it, and as you face it, learn from it.”

Panay said it’s possible to recover from all sorts of failures, even catastrophic ones, noting that he experienced one himself at Microsoft. He described the launch of the Surface RT, Microsoft’s first tablet computer, as a significant failure during his tenure at the company, one that ultimately led to a nearly $1 billion write-down.

“I remember being on the front cover of a newspaper, and it just said failure,” Panay said. “But, here’s the thing, it was easy to admit failure. The trick was, and always is, did you harvest the learnings and understand what happened? All right. What did you learn? Because the failure wasn’t that moment. It was decisions that led up to it two years before that, whether the software wasn’t complete or the inventory was wrong or how we balanced into retail. There were all these steps along the way.”

He said founders need to be willing to understand what went wrong, and avoid making excuses, and ultimately accept the failure.

“Here’s the other side of it,” he said. “You want to succeed, yeah? You take that failure, but you don’t let go of your vision. That’s it. Surface has done pretty well. You don’t let go of your vision. You don’t break it.”

Panay emphasized the importance of staying committed to a vision, learning from experience, and moving quickly. He believes that by embracing failure and learning from setbacks, founders can adapt and make progress faster, even as they encounter new obstacles.

“It goes back to the same fundamental, like, have you learned?” he said. “Were you learning along the way? Because if you were learning, then you just change your vector. Usually, it’s not 180 degrees. Usually, it’s just 30 degrees. Take your lessons learned, change a little bit, adapt your vision where it needs to be, and then go. I believe there’s people that hang on too long, but it’s because they haven’t accepted the moment of failure at all.”

articles.title: Anna Faris Was “Hurt” By Chuck Lorre’s Comments About Her ‘Mom’ Exit: “Yikes”
articles.summary: Six years after announcing her departure from CBS’s Mom, Anna Faris has reacted to Chuck Lorre’s comments about her exit. On Thursday, the actress shared a s...
articles.body:
Six years after announcing her departure from CBS's Mom , Anna Faris has reacted to Chuck Lorre's comments about her exit.

On Thursday, the actress shared a statement explaining that she "never took a day of [the show] for granted" after series co-creator Lorre wrote in his new memoir Sitcom that he "was, in fact, correct" about his initial reluctance to cast her as Christy Plunkett in the sitcom.

"Yikes. Yes, I read a few things. I really didn't see that coming. Of course it hurts," she began in a statement on Instagram . "Chuck gave me a job I loved, and for seven years I never took a day of it for granted. I'm proud of what we made together, and nothing changes how grateful I am for those people and those years."

Faris continued: "I've been sober for a year and a half. I was on a show about recovery, and then I lived it. Now I'm healthy, I'm working, and I'm happier than I've been in a long time. If anyone reading this is where I was, I hope that's useful. It gets better. I'm proof."

Premiering in 2013, Faris starred in the first seven seasons of Mom as Christy, a recovering alcoholic who struggles to maintain a job, her family and her sobriety as her mom Bonnie (Allison Janney), who's also in recovery, moves in with her.

Faris left the show in 2020 to "pursue new opportunities," leaving Janney as the sole lead for the eighth and final season, which ended in 2021.

In an excerpt from Sitcom , Lorre wrote: "I wasn't sure Anna would be appropriate for this kind of material. Then I thought about how badly I'd bungled my working relationship with Charlie Sheen."

After his experience with Charlie Sheen on Two and a Half Men , Lorre recalled conceding, "Someone's personal life is none of my business. The mom in Mom would be, and should be, Anna Faris."

Lorre added: "As the years went by, it became apparent that my initial reluctance to hire Anna was, in fact, correct. After six years, she left the show for mysterious reasons that were not mysterious to anyone on the show."

articles.title: ‘SNL’ Star Michael Che Reacts to Shane Gillis’ Controversial Monologue: “That’s Comedy”
articles.summary: Gillis drew heat for a joke he made about women in the gym while recently hosting the NBC sketch comedy program.
articles.body:
Michael Che has been preparing for potential questions about Shane Gillis' controversial monologue on Saturday Night Live last weekend, and the moment has arrived.

"I gotta do more press this week to promote the special. Wonder what every fucking question's gonna be about," Che wrote on his Instagram earlier this week, regarding the press tour for his new Netflix stand-up special, Michael Che: Shot in Minnesota . "Thanks a lot Shane."

For context, after hosting the NBC sketch comedy program on Saturday, Gillis drew heat over his joke about women working out.

"I haven't been to the gym in so long, I didn't know women just dress like whores now," Gillis said to the live audience. "Look, I'm sorry, there's no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I've seen it. The shorts? Have you seen the shorts? They're neon, like, artificial bait-colored? And the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don't look. You're not allowed to look. For real, don't look, because they are filming. I'm in the background of like 10 TikToks right now."

Despite being adamant about not being interested in weighing in on the discourse, Che, who anchors "Weekend Update" with Colin Jost on SNL , was asked on the Today show Thursday about the controversy.

"That's comedy," he said. "It's like, you think it's funny and some people don't."

He was later asked if he laughed at Gillis' joke about women, to which Che replied, "I was at cue cards actually, thinking about what I was gonna say that was gonna make people upset. I didn't even see it until the next day."

Che isn't a stranger to controversial jokes, especially during his bi-annual joke swap with Jost on SNL , where the jokes can get quite dicey.

"That's why I can't criticize anybody for swinging and missing because I've definitely swung and missed too," the comedian said on Today . "I try to keep that heat off of me."

After drawing some backlash for his remarks on the NBC morning program, Che responded to a fan on Instagram who asked why he had no problem calling Kanye "Ye" West out in the past, but not Gillis.

"That's a fair question. Especially since when I called Kanye out, I did so privately. I had no idea he was filming. Point being, when I have a problem with someone I address them in person. Not thru the media. I'm not gonna drag someone on the Today show, when I can just text them. It's a courtesy that's been extended to me in the past, and I like to pay that forward."

Following Gillis' monologue, Dan Levy was among some celebrities who slammed the comedian over his joke about women at the gym. "Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists. There's a difference there," the Schitt's Creek co-creator and star wrote in part.

Levy added in his Instagram post, "I'm speechless that something like that can exist on live national television. And to be perfectly honest, more men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it's complacency that has created the environment in which women are sexually assaulted and it's a 'conversation' as opposed to a 'crime.'"

Former SNL castmember Ego Nwodim also responded with a photo of herself at the gym with the caption, "Whore reporting for duty."

articles.summary: Google has announced a major expansion of its Android Earthquake Alerts System, extending the feature from 98 countries and regions to more than 200 while
articles.body: Google has announced a major expansion of its Android Earthquake Alerts System, extending the feature from 98 countries and regions to more than 200 while introducing additional information in earthquake warnings to help users respond more effectively during emergencies. The company also added that the system has managed to deliver more than one billion earthquake alerts since its launch in 2021, making it what Google describes as the world’s largest mobile-based earthquake detection network. The expanded coverage will bring alerts to more locations including Panama and Guatemala, among others.The announcement was highlighted by Google CEO Sundar Pichai, who said the technology has already aided people during critical moments. In a post on X, Pichai noted that the system has sent over one billion alerts since 2021 and is now expanding from 98 to nearly 200 countries and regions. He also pointed to this year's earthquakes in Venezuela, saying millions of people outside the epicentre received alerts and were able to take cover before the shaking began. “Since launching in 2021, our Android Earthquake Alerts System has sent 1B+ alerts. Now we’re expanding the system from 98 to nearly 200 countries and regions. Proud how this technology can help in moments that really matter. As one example, when the devastating earthquakes hit Venezuela this year, millions of people outside the epicenter got alerts and could take cover before the shaking began,” wrote Pichai in a post.New details added to earthquake alertsAlongside the geographic expansion, Google is enhancing its "Be Ready" earthquake alert with more contextual information. In the coming months, users will see a map showing the radius of detected shaking, the estimated earthquake magnitude, recommended actions, and a button to access more information as details become available.Android users in supported regions may receive one of three alert types depending on the expected intensity of shaking. The "Be Aware" alert is designed for estimated light shaking, while "Be Ready" provides advance notice of stronger shaking and encourages users to prepare. The highest-level "Take Action" alert appears full-screen and offers immediate safety guidance for moderate to heavy shaking.Designed to provide precious seconds of warningGoogle said even a few seconds of advance notice can be crucial during an earthquake, giving people time to take cover and protect themselves. The Android Earthquake Alerts System uses mobile devices to help detect seismic activity and deliver warnings before strong shaking reaches users.The company said its safety-focused products play an important role during natural disasters, adding that the latest expansion aims to provide more people with potentially life-saving information when they need it most.You use AI every day.
